There were TONS of small moths, caterpillars, and a pupae in oaks and other hardwood shrubs and trees along the northern boundary, while the southern boundary had some blooming (Joe) Bidens that attracted several butterflies. I tried to photograph every moth food plant in case some species are not known to be moth hosts, as well as to hopefully narrow down the moth identification possibilities. Moths were so abundant that walking by nearly every low-growing oak meant that 4, 5, 6, or more moths would fly out. Some landed on my shirt, pants, or hand! I also found a super-cool leafhopper that hopefully can be identified to species.

The park seemed to include centuries-old pines (I think Longleaf Pine but I'm not positive) and Live Oaks; I was not expecting either.

As this is an urban park, there were many exotic plants growing in it. However, I believe that none were intentionally planted -- rather, they naturalized -- so that all plants should be Research-Gradable.

I used my Panasonic Lumix FZ80 for all non-macro photographs, and I used my Samsung A52 cell phone for macro-photography.

The weather at my arrival was sunny and 73 degrees ("feels like" 73) with a light breeze. I left around 1635 and battled traffic all the way home.

I am submitting 180 records from Kapok Park.

description:
With Erik Haney; Gallus Quigley was also present, as were others who arrived later; a finally successful search for the Yellow-headed Caracara! With the caracara recently alternating between visiting two picnic pavilions (Angelfish and Pelican) 1,000 feet apart, Erik and I intended to split up, with each of us at a different pavilion. We first visited Angelfish Pavilion and then Pelican Pavilion, neither with any sign of the caracara. After we saw Gallus Quigley at Pelican Pavilion, Erik went to Angelfish Pavilion and remained there while Gallus remained at Pelican, and I shuttled between the two pavilions every 10 or so minutes. The weather at the start was sunny, 77 degrees ("feels like" 77), and breezy.

Both pavilions were full of people barbequing and picnicking (and playing Spanish music at various decibels), and there was a wedding party at Angelfish. The beach between the pavilions was absolutely packed with people.

At 1902, the caracara flew into Pelican Pavilion from the direction of the FIU Biscayne campus. Erik called me to say that it had flown in and was close to us. I told Gallus and three other birders who had just arrived about Erik's call, and we found the caracara quickly, sitting maybe 20 feet up in a fig in the center of the pavilion, with people everywhere. We were nearly directly under the fig tree. After a few minutes, the caracara flew north to Angelfish Pavilion, and we raced over there for better views. The caracara landed in another fig tree directly over the wedding party with at least 40 people, including the bride, groom, best men, bridesmaids, and others! It was pretty crazy. After 6 minutes, the caracara flew east, and we quickly lost sight of it.

We left shortly afterward because park rangers were starting to clear out the park in time for its 1930 (sunset) closing. (The wedding party must have had special permission to remain later, since they had not touched any of their food by 1915).

Erik and I quickly headed north then west, stopping at the Miccosukee Travel Center in Broward County for gas and munchies. Erik arrived home in St. Petersburg at 0014 Sunday morning, and I arrived home at 0130.

It was an exhausting and epic day.

description:
With Dave Goodwin and Erik Haney, plus 4 others; an unsuccessful search for the Yellow-headed Caracara. We arrived in the dark and stayed for 3.5 hours. The weather at the start was clear (pre-sunrise), 70 degrees ("feels like" 71), and breezy. We spread out, with Dave at the "bait shop," Erik just south of the Bill Bird Marina building, and me ranging from a bit farther north to 0.4 miles farther north (across a large grassy area to the next parking lot north). None of us saw any sign of the caracara. I slowly walked my way back south, along the west shoreline; by the time I met up with Dave and Erik, the 4 others had headed home. Dave had Easter plans with family, so he too left. Erik and I left Haulover Park at 1002 and drove around the FIU Biscayne campus to the west for 33 minutes.

I recorded 20 bird species while in the park; the best bird was the Gray Kingbird that I repeatedly heard (and audio-recorded) but never saw. It was roosting in one of the Coconut Palms north of the Bill Bird Marina building, and it must have left without me seeing it fly away, as I never heard it again.

description:
I had the opportunity to watch this squirrel collect and bury several findings of food dropped from the bird feeders.  It would take a nibble, carry it a few feet away, scratch at the dirt to dig a hole about 1 inch deep, and then cram it's nose in and drop the food into it.  It would then scoop the dirt back to cover the hole, and tap it down a few times.  It seemed to push it's front paws down onto the hole to seal it up, while stretching a bit to look up and around and ensure no burglars had seen it's secret treasure spot.

One time. I watched it dig up some food, eat part of it, then dig a new home about 1 foot away and bury it.  I wonder if this was their own stash being relocated, or stolen from a different squirrel's stash.

When I walked outside later, I saw about 2 little dark spots on the soil, all the places it had dug it's tiny little treasure spots among the bark dust.   I wonder if I will be fortunate enough to witness their retrieval at some future date.

description:
Partially cloudy, ~75F
Ran around in small bursts, then would sit up and look around. He was between the apartment building and the parking lot.

A Gulfwatch 14-19 hours after the passage of Hurricane Helene, maybe 80 miles west in the Gulf of Mexico. I was astounded that the park was open and that there was almost no standing water anywhere from Spring Hill -- only the usual spots along Hudson Avenue at Old Dixie Highway were flooded with maybe 4-5 inches of water. Several people -- mostly sightseers -- were already at the park at my arrival. All the picnic tables had been removed, so there was nothing but a concrete slab in each pavilion. Christine Rowland joined me for an hourish, Joe Colontonio dropped by for a few minutes, and Dave Bowman joined me for about 3.5 hours. The weather at the start was sunny and windy (12-15 mph) from the west-southwest;  considering the massive destruction less than 100 miles to the north, it was quite a beautiful morning. The sidewalk was covered with sand and the walkway in front of Sam's Beach Bar was inundated with choppy waves, but there was no water over the seawall. It really was lovely watching conditions, even though I had to stand the entire morning.

Even though I am uploading screenshots of my camera photographs, I will go back into each record to add a timestamp -- something I have never before done for so many records. I am submitting 92 records from this stationary Gulfwatch.

As always, I keep a field notebook for every trip, including birds seen but not photographed -- even though such reports now mean nothing to me.

Mallard: 3
Blue-winged Teal: 7, 25, 24, 4, and 1, all southbound
Brown Pelican: 11, 2, 1, 2, 1, 15 (northbound!), 1, 1, 4, 3, 6, and 5, mostly southbound
American White Pelican: 2 heading west into the Gulf
Double-crested Cormorant: 80 estimated, 50 in the Casuarinas at their roost and maybe 30 others variously, all locals
Anhinga: 1 local
Magnificent Frigatebird: 11, 4, 2, 2, 3, 4, 1, and 3, all southbound
Great Blue Heron 1 and 1, southbound
Snowy Egret, 1 and 1, locals
Tricolored Heron, 1, southbound
American Oystercatcher, 1, southbound (not photographed)
American Avocet: 30 and 4, southbound
Semipalmeted Plover: 1, southbound
Killdeer, 1 (not photographed), local
(Western Willet): 1, local
Least Sandpiper: 1, southbound, stopped to forage
Sanderling: 1, southbound (not photographed)
Laughing Gull: 50 estimated, variously, all locals?
Royal Tern: 25-30, mostly singles, mostly southbound
Sandwich (Cabot's) Tern: 60-70, mostly singles, mostly southbound. My highest count for Pasco County.
Black Tern: 1, southbound
Black Skimmer: 9, southbound then northbound minutes later
Belted Kingfisher: 1 (not photographed), local
Eurasian Collared-Dove: 1
Mourning Dove: 2
Peregrine Falcon (!), 1; it flew in from the Gulf -- its first landfall in hundreds of miles?
Barn Swallow: 1, 1, and 1, all southbound, all before 0830
Fish Crow: 1 vocal, 2 vocal (not photographed; audio-recorded by Merlin)
Boat-tailed Grackle: 10-12, disappeared quickly, local

Dave and I were going to leave around 1130, but then we decided to stay until 1200, at which time the winds increased, and more terns flew by. We decided to stay another hour, but Pasco County sheriffs kicked out everybody at 1220 (apparently the park service wanted to clean up the park -- not that there was much to do). We tried to find a fast-food restaurant that was open, but we gave up after two Burger Kings and a Wendy's were closed; a McDonald's was open but there must have been 15 cars in the drive-through, so we headed home separately.

description: One deuterostome I was able to identify is called the, "Eastern Gray Squirrel" (sciurus carolinensis). This species belongs to the phylum Chordata. They are native to the eastern and western of the United States. They can be identified through their grayish fur coated tinged with brown and white underparts. The underparts include their chest and belly. They also show hints of red and brown that runs along their back. In addition, their tail is a mix of gray and white. They are usually bushy and fluffy due to the hairs surrounding the tail. They are also typically tipped with a silvery-white fringe. The tail helps them balance when they climb and can be used for communication. Their forelimbs and hindlimbs are also essential towards helping them jump between trees and eating. They rely on nuts, seeds, berries, and fungi to survive. They have an average body length of 9-12 and the tail adds about 7.5-10 inches to their body. They have a rounded head with black eyes which enhances their vision and hearing. The nose and mouth are slightly pink. Their long whiskers are also important in sensing their surroundings.

description:
For my observation of black and gray squirrels, I documented both color morphs of the Eastern Gray Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) in a local park. The gray squirrel is typically recognized for its gray fur and bushy tail, while the black morph of the same species exhibits a darker coat, ranging from dark gray to almost black. Both morphs exhibit similar behaviors, such as foraging for nuts and climbing trees with agility, although the black squirrels tend to be more elusive.

I captured high-quality photographs of both the black and gray morphs side by side, highlighting the distinct fur coloration differences. The initial observation was rated casual grade due to its clear identification and documentation.
This observation is an excellent example of how casual observations can be validated by the broader community, ensuring the accuracy of species data and enriching our understanding of wildlife in urban environments.

North Pinellas Christmas Bird Count with Mia Majetschak. While Mia covered her yard and a small park, I drove to Philippe Park (during daylight!). The temperature at the start was sunny, 55 degrees ("feels like" 53) and breezy (NNW at 12 mph). The tide was high. Mia and I met at the boat ramp around 0820 and after scoping the (nearly birdless) northwestern part of Tampa Bay, we walked the trails away from the shoreline. The damage to the park from Hurricanes Helene and Milton was relatively light, but several large oaks (decades old) were toppled. We did well here, finding owls (the incubating Great Horned Owl, a local celebrity) and three Eastern Screech-Owls that responded to our playback to attract landbirds -- I don't know that I have ever had 3 Eastern Screech-Owls respond to playback at any one spot before -- and numerous passerines, including a Western Tanager, the highlight of the CBC. (I got one headless and several out-of-focus photos. Fortunately Mia refound the tanager on 22 Dec and got definitive photos. We left at 1220 and got lunch before returning later to survey the southern half of the park.
